summary: A write-up of the TELNET command at Host LL for the CP/CMS time-sharing system, which could run in half or full duplex and with ASCII or EBCDIC codes. It describes keyboard conventions for IBM 2741 terminals and local control commands, including reading input from a file. The text says it was not reviewed for public release.

plainLanguage.summary: A guide to a program that lets people at a certain computer connect to other computers, including special keys for a typewriter-like terminal.

subtitle: A guide to accessing remote systems from an IBM mainframe using the TELNET protocol.

tldr.problem: Users at Host LL (a 360/67 running CP/CMS) needed a way to connect to and use other systems on the ARPANET, but their local terminals and character sets did not match the Network Virtual Terminal standard.
tldr.mechanism: The TELNET command translates between the local EBCDIC character set used by IBM systems and the ASCII used by the network, supports both half-duplex and full-duplex modes, and includes control commands for special functions like file input/output and terminal control.
tldr.outcome: Users could connect to other ARPANET systems while working in their native environment, though the implementation was restricted to ARPA network use and not reviewed for public release.

today: RFC 452 documents a local TELNET implementation for a specific system and character set. It is a historical record of how early systems bridged incompatible terminal and character encoding standards. This implementation and the systems it served are no longer in operation.

sections.title: TELNET at Host LL
sections.content:
RFC 452 documents the TELNET command implementation at Host LL, an IBM System/360 Model 67 running CP/CMS at Lincoln Laboratory. This writeup was not reviewed for public release and was intended solely for ARPANET use.

The command allows users at Host LL to connect to terminal-oriented systems elsewhere on the network. It supports half-duplex and full-duplex modes, as well as ASCII and EBCDIC character encoding, making it possible to bridge the gap between IBM systems and the ASCII-based Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Host LL was an IBM computer that wanted to connect to other computers on the network, but IBM computers use different character codes. This document explains how the connection worked.

sections.title: Connection and Modes
sections.content:
The TELNET command takes a host name or address, a tag to identify the local connection, and optional parameters for the operating mode. Once a connection is established between Host LL and a serving site, keyboard input from the local user is sent to the remote system, and output from the remote system is displayed on the local terminal.

The command supports two duplex modes: in half-duplex mode, the keyboard locks after sending a line and unlocks when output arrives (useful for compatibility with line-oriented systems like EBCDIC terminals). In full-duplex mode, the keyboard is always available, and a null line is used to temporarily lock it to receive output.
sections.plainLanguage: When you run TELNET, you pick which computer to reach, and your keyboard input goes there while the remote computer's replies come back to your screen.

sections.title: Character Translation
sections.content:
The central challenge of this implementation is character encoding. The NVT protocol requires 8-bit ASCII, but Host LL uses EBCDIC. The TELNET command includes complete mapping tables between EBCDIC and ASCII, handling both printable characters and control codes.

An IBM 2741 terminal keyboard does not have all the ASCII keys (such as square brackets, braces, and the caret). The TELNET implementation solves this by allowing users to enter a control character, followed by another character, to produce ASCII codes not present on the keyboard. For example, pressing the control character plus 'a' might produce a left square bracket. The RFC includes detailed mappings for all 128 ASCII codes.
sections.plainLanguage: IBM and the network use different codes for letters and symbols. TELNET translates between them, and it shows how to type network codes using an IBM keyboard that does not have all the right keys.

sections.title: Control Commands and File Transfer
sections.content:
Beyond simple character input and output, the TELNET command at Host LL includes control commands that allow users to change modes, send TELNET control codes, and redirect input and output to files. A line beginning with the control character followed by a space is interpreted as a control command.

Control commands include: CONTROL x to change the control character, CLOSE to terminate the connection, INPUT to read from a file instead of the terminal, and OUTPUT to write to a file. These commands provide a rudimentary file transfer facility, allowing users to upload and download data by routing it through local files.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides typing and receiving text, TELNET has special commands that let you read input from a file or save output to a file, which is a simple way to move files between computers.
